The OP dutifully reposts the canon: the GameStop timeline, naked-shorting exposés, fail-to-deliver primers, and the investor portal nobody visits. clips.text_en_c2: Once again, the familiar /biz/ GME general has resurfaced, rehashing the same well-worn canon that aficionados of the saga have recited ad nauseam for years. clips.text_zh: 又係BTC。橫盤兩星期唔理，pump 15%就全部人衝入去。wtf 永遠都係咁 lol 幾時先學到教訓
clips.text_en_b1: /biz/ anon asks why everyone wants to buy BTC after the pump. The price does nothing for weeks and nobody cares. Then it jumps 15% and suddenly everyone wants in. The post points out that people always want to buy after the move already happened.
clips.source_hint: /biz/ rant about chasing BTC after a pump
clips.text_en_b2: Another /biz/ post is poking fun at crypto herd behaviour, questioning why buyers suddenly pile in after BTC has already moved. According to the OP, the price essentially flatlines for weeks and nobody bats an eyelid, yet once it pumps around 15% out of nowhere, FOMO kicks in and everyone rushes the exit door. The poster points out this pattern keeps repeating itself, and asks when people will finally learn the lesson.
clips.text_en_c1: An anon on /biz/ poses what is by now a rhetorical question: why does retail invariably chase Bitcoin immediately after the move? For roughly a fortnight, price action was directionless, and sentiment was apathetic; the moment BTC surged some fifteen percent, however, the very same participants who dismissed it scrambled to enter positions. The post crystallises a behavioural pattern that traders themselves acknowledge yet never seem to internalise. Whether this constitutes FOMO in its purest form or simply crowd-induced capitulation is, evidently, beside the point.
clips.text_en_c2: A /biz/ anon, palpably weary of the cyclical theatrics, poses what is by now a rhetorical inquiry: why does the retail cohort invariably capitulate to FOMO the moment Bitcoin registers a discernible move? The price idles, listless and unremarkable, for a fortnight; not a soul blinks. Then, with the predictability of a Greek tragedy, BTC surges fifteen percent and the platforms buckle under the weight of late entrants scrambling aboard a vessel that has, by definition, already departed. The poster observes, with no small measure of exasperation, that human nature — at least within this particular subreddit — appears constitutionally incapable of buying the rumour rather than the fact, of accumulating before the breakout rather than afterwards.

clips.text_zh: 有條片講24/7 AI agent寫code，一個月push 1000個PR。ok 而家連我自己份工都驚畀AI搶 🧐 考牌有用啲嘅話…
clips.text_en_b1: Anon posted a YouTube video about AI agent coding. The woman in the video says she runs a bunch of agents 24/7 and pushes around 1000 PRs a month. The poster thinks her method is just trial and error, not based on how LLMs actually work. He says the right way is to study how the tech works first.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread debating AI agents writing code 24/7
clips.text_en_b2: Anon shared a YouTube clip in which a developer claims to run AI coding agents around the clock, allegedly pushing close to 1000 pull requests a month. While the numbers sound impressive, the OP reckons her method is essentially trial and error dressed up as a workflow, rather than anything grounded in how large language models actually operate. He argues the smarter approach is understanding the underlying tech before throwing agents at production.
clips.text_en_c1: A clip circulating on /g/ features a developer claiming to operate AI coding agents around the clock, allegedly merging close to a thousand pull requests monthly. The OP, however, remains sceptical, contending that her methodology amounts to little more than trial-and-error prompting rather than any principled understanding of how large language models actually function. He insists that the proper approach requires first internalising the underlying architecture before attempting to orchestrate autonomous systems, a distinction he feels the broader discourse routinely overlooks entirely.
clips.text_en_c2: A new /g/ submission features a YouTube lecture in which the presenter extols the virtues of perpetually operational AI agents that, in her telling, submit roughly a thousand pull requests monthly, presumably while the operator sleeps. The original poster, however, is unmoved by the spectacle, arguing with some justification that her methodology amounts to little more than stochastic trial-and-error — a brute-force engagement divorced from any rigorous understanding of how large language models actually function. He contends, persuasively enough, that the prudent practitioner ought first to internalise the underlying architecture before unleashing autonomous code generators into production, lest competence be sacrificed at the altar of throughput.

clips.text_zh: /pol/有人話西歐最ungrateful。美軍解放過佢哋，依家當冇事。東歐起碼畀蘇聯搞到仆街。睇完好似講緊香港同美國關係 😅
clips.text_en_b1: /pol/ thread says Western Europeans are the most ungrateful people on the planet. The OP argues Americans actually liberated Western Europe, while Central and Eastern Europe just got swapped from one totalitarian occupation to another under the Soviets. He asks anons to imagine France or the Netherlands under Soviet-style rule today.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ rant comparing Western and Eastern Europe after WWII
clips.text_en_b2: A /pol/ thread argues that Western Europeans are arguably the most ungrateful people on the planet, since US forces liberated them from Nazi occupation, yet they largely take that sacrifice for granted. By contrast, Central and Eastern Europeans were simply traded from one totalitarian regime to another under Soviet control. The OP challenges anons to picture France or the Netherlands living under Soviet-style governance today, and the parallels to Hong Kong are hard to miss.
clips.text_en_c1: A /pol/ thread contends that Western Europeans rank among the most ungrateful populations on earth. The OP's central claim is that American forces genuinely liberated Western Europe from Nazi tyranny, whereas Central and Eastern Europeans merely exchanged one totalitarian occupier for another under Soviet domination. He invites anons to envisage France or the Netherlands subjected to Moscow-aligned governance today, presumably so they might recalibrate their assessment of historical indebtedness, which the poster considers conspicuously absent from contemporary European discourse.
clips.text_en_c2: A /pol/ thread advances the somewhat inflammatory thesis that Western Europeans constitute the most ingratitudinous polity on the contemporary geopolitical stage. The original poster contends, with characteristic bluntness, that Americans actually liberated Western Europe from fascist subjugation, an undertaking for which their gratitude has proved, shall we say, understated. Central and Eastern Europe, by contrast, merely exchanged one totalitarian overlord for another, a distinction that apparently confers upon them a measure of moral absolution. He invites anons to contemplate, however briefly, the prospect of metropolitan Paris or Rotterdam languishing beneath Soviet-style autocracy today — a thought experiment whose implications he evidently considers self-evident.

clips.text_en_b1: /v/ thread says: she benches 70kg, if you are benching anything below that you should be ashamed. The poster flexes a personal number and dares anyone under it to cope. Classic /v/ shitposting that somehow turned into a gym argument overnight.
clips.source_hint: /v/ bench press flex post from the front page
clips.text_en_b2: A /v/ thread has erupted into gym bragging, with one anon claiming she benches 70kg and suggesting anyone lifting less should feel ashamed. The original poster threw out his own number as a flex and dared anyone below it to cope. What started as typical shitposting somehow snowballed into a full-blown bench press debate overnight, and now every skinnyfat guy on the board is checking his numbers.
clips.text_en_c1: A /v/ thread has devolved into what can only be described as a bench-press humiliation ritual. The original poster, evidently a woman who benches seventy kilograms, has effectively dared anyone lifting below that threshold to remain silent. She then volunteered her own number, daring underperformers to cope in her replies. What began as routine shitposting somehow metastasised overnight into a fully-fledged strength-training argument, drawing in gymbros who treat internet forums as though they were competition platforms, which, regrettably, they often are.
clips.text_en_c2: A /v/ thread has, in a feat of genre-transcendence, devolved into gymnasium discourse, with the original poster loftily asserting that any individual failing to bench-press seventy kilograms should be roundly ashamed of themselves. She proffers her own number as a not-so-modest benchmark beneath which no self-respecting lifter ought to descend. What began as conventional shitposting has, through that alchemical process peculiar to anonymous forums, mutated overnight into a spirited — if numerically inflected — debate about pressing capacity. Lurkers of more modest accomplishments, it must be said, have perused the proceedings with a mixture of amusement and existential dread, bracing themselves for the inevitable summons to the comments section.

clips.text_zh: /fit/有人cut緊，三個月跌45磅但甩晒肌肉。連squats都做唔到，心臟頂唔順。我下個月都打算cut…睇完驚 🧐
clips.text_en_b1: /fit/ anon is losing weight fast but cannot lift heavy anymore. He dropped 45 pounds in 3 months, lost muscle and strength, and gets exhausted doing squats. He can barely eat more than a couple of times a day and has to force-feed himself every morning just to hit calories.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ poster complaining about cutting killing his lifts
clips.text_en_b2: An /fit/ anon is cutting aggressively and paying the price, having shed roughly 45 pounds in three months, but the muscle has clearly vanished alongside the fat. He can no longer handle squats without his heart rate spiking, gets winded mid-set, and barely manages two proper meals a day. Force-feeding himself breakfast just to hit basic calories has become routine, and honestly the whole thing looks like a cautionary tale.
clips.text_en_c1: A /fit/ anon recounts the grim consequences of an aggressive cut: roughly forty-five pounds shed over three months, accompanied by an alarming erosion of both muscle and strength. Compound movements such as squats have become genuinely taxing, and cardiovascular exertion leaves him utterly depleted. He reports being able to consume solid food only sporadically, forcing himself to eat each morning merely to approach his calorie target. Anyone contemplating a similar protocol should, he implies, proceed with considerable caution indeed.
clips.text_en_c2: A /fit/ anon, presently in the throes of an aggressive cut, catalogues the somewhat discouraging consequences of his regimen with admirable candour. Within a mere three months he has shed forty-five pounds, a figure that on paper bespeaks triumph but in practice has translated into the precipitous erosion of muscular mass and the kind of strength attrition that renders even moderate squats an exercise in cardiovascular distress. He confesses, with no evident embarrassment, to being able to consume sustenance only a handful of times daily, each morning's caloric intake constituting a Sisyphean exercise in self-coercion. The thread thus serves as a cautionary rejoinder to those contemplating similar pursuits without due preparation.

clips.text_zh: /a/有人貼中國AI整到睇得過嘅動畫slide show，仲有人用嚟adapt niche漫畫。ok 以後動畫公司都畀AI搞掂？考牌冇用 😩
clips.text_en_b1: /a/ thread about Chinese AI generating watchable anime slideshows. The OP links a YouTube sample and says people are already using the tech to adapt niche manga that would never get a real anime. Anons are debating whether this kills studios or just helps small creators.
clips.text_en_b2: /a/ is buzzing about Chinese AI tools producing anime slideshows that are, surprisingly, fairly watchable, with the OP linking a YouTube sample as evidence. Several anons note creators are already using this tech to adapt obscure manga that would never realistically receive a proper studio production. The thread has split into two camps: those convinced this technology will eventually displace traditional studios, and others who see it as a lifeline for small creators.
clips.text_en_c1: A /a/ thread showcases Chinese AI-generated anime that, against all reasonable expectation, has attained a level of watchability once thought impossible. The OP links a YouTube sample demonstrating slideshow-style output, while contributors note that the technology is already being deployed to adapt obscure manga titles that studios would never commercially greenlight. Anons remain divided: some view this development as the death knell for traditional animation houses, whereas others regard it as democratisation that simply empowers smaller creators operating without institutional backing.
clips.text_en_c2: A /a/ submission showcases Chinese-developed AI rendering sequences of sufficient fidelity to qualify, however provisionally, as watchable anime — at least in the generous estimation of an audience long inured to diminished expectations. The original poster, having linked a representative YouTube sample, observes that enterprising individuals are already leveraging the technology to adapt niche manga that, under any conventional studio calculus, would never receive the animation treatment. Anons are presently engaged in spirited debate as to whether this development portends obsolescence for established studios or merely democratises production for marginalised creators, a question whose answer will doubtless depend upon whom one asks — and when.
